questions.t: Richard Sloan's 1996 study found that the accrual part of earnings persists less into future earnings than the cash flow part.
questions.f: Richard Sloan's 1996 study found that the accrual part of earnings persists more into future earnings than the cash flow part.
questions.x: Sloan showed accruals are the less persistent piece of earnings, yet prices treated both pieces alike; a long low-accrual, short high-accrual portfolio earned about 10.4% in year one. That gap is the 'accrual anomaly' analysts now screen for.

questions.t: Under accrual accounting, a major equipment purchase is capitalized and depreciated over its useful life rather than expensed when paid for.
questions.f: Under accrual accounting, a major equipment purchase is expensed in full in the period it is paid for rather than depreciated over its useful life.
questions.x: Because the matching principle ties expenses to the periods they help earn revenue, long-lived assets are capitalized and spread over their useful lives through depreciation. Expensing the full cost on payment is how the cash basis treats it.

questions.t: The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act let most taxpayers under a $25 million average annual gross receipts test use the cash method.
questions.f: The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act let most taxpayers under a $50 million average annual gross receipts test use the cash method.
questions.x: The 2017 law raised the Sec. 448(c) gross receipts threshold for the cash method from $5 million to $25 million, widening who can skip accrual accounting for tax. $50 million was never the test.

questions.t: Michael Jensen and William Meckling formalized agency costs in a 1976 Journal of Financial Economics paper on the theory of the firm.
questions.f: Ronald Coase and Oliver Williamson formalized agency costs in a 1976 Journal of Financial Economics paper on the theory of the firm.
questions.x: Jensen and Meckling's 1976 'Theory of the Firm' paper defined agency costs and tied them to the separation of ownership and control. It also recast the firm as a nexus of contracts among individuals.

questions.t: Agency costs are the sum of the principal's monitoring costs, the agent's bonding costs and the residual loss that remains after both.
questions.f: Agency costs are the sum of the principal's monitoring costs, the agent's salary and the residual loss that remains after both.
questions.x: Jensen and Meckling split agency costs into monitoring (spent by the principal), bonding (spent by the agent to reassure the principal) and residual loss, the welfare still lost because the agent's choices differ. An agent's ordinary pay is not one of the three.

questions.t: Jensen's 1986 free cash flow argument holds that debt can discipline managers by committing excess cash to creditors, much like paying dividends.
questions.f: Jensen's 1986 free cash flow argument holds that equity issues can discipline managers by committing excess cash to creditors, much like paying dividends.
questions.x: Jensen argued conflicts are worst where cash exceeds positive-NPV projects, and debt forces that cash out to lenders. He used this to explain 1980s takeovers and LBOs in cash-rich industries such as oil.

questions.t: By early 1914, Ford's moving assembly lines finished a Model T chassis every 93 minutes, versus about 12½ hours with stationary assembly.
questions.f: By early 1914, Ford's moving assembly lines finished a Model T chassis every 93 minutes, versus about 3 hours with stationary assembly.
questions.x: Moving the work to the worker, tried first on flywheel magnetos in 1913 and then the whole chassis, cut assembly time roughly eightfold. The savings funded price cuts that expanded demand.

questions.t: After Ford's 1914 five-dollar day, annual worker turnover fell from 370 percent in 1913 to 54 percent in 1914.
questions.f: After Ford's 1914 five-dollar day, annual worker turnover rose from 54 percent in 1913 to 370 percent in 1914.
questions.x: In 1913 Ford hired over 50,000 men to keep about 13,600 on the payroll. Raff and Summers found the near-doubled wage slashed turnover and absenteeism, which is why the case is classic evidence for efficiency-wage theory.

questions.t: In the 1920s General Motors overtook the Model T by offering annual model changes, trade-ins and installment buying.
questions.f: In the 1920s General Motors overtook the Model T by offering a single unchanging model at an ever-lower price.
questions.x: Ford bet on one nearly unchanged car built at huge volume; that was Ford's strategy, not GM's. Under Alfred Sloan, GM competed on variety and novelty, and Chevrolet was outselling the Model T by early 1927.

questions.t: Jean-Charles Rochet and Jean Tirole formalized two-sided markets in a 2003 paper whose model was built around the payment-card industry.
questions.f: Jean-Charles Rochet and Jean Tirole formalized two-sided markets in a 2003 paper whose model was built around the newspaper industry.
questions.x: Their 2003 Journal of the European Economic Association paper modelled how card platforms split prices between cardholders and merchants. Armstrong's 2006 paper later extended the analysis to competing platforms.

questions.t: When one side of a two-sided market multi-homes, platforms compete hardest for the single-homing side and can charge the multi-homing side more.
questions.f: When one side of a two-sided market multi-homes, platforms compete hardest for the multi-homing side and can charge the single-homing side more.
questions.x: A single-homing user is reachable only through the platform it joins, so platforms fight for those users and then charge the other side for access to them. That is Armstrong's 'competitive bottleneck' result.

questions.t: In Ohio v. American Express (2018), a 5–4 Supreme Court majority defined the card market to include both cardholders and merchants.
questions.f: In Ohio v. American Express (2018), a 5–4 Supreme Court majority defined the card market to include merchants only, not cardholders.
questions.x: The majority treated card networks as two-sided transaction platforms and found no proven net harm from Amex's anti-steering rules. Justice Breyer's dissent argued the two sides are complements and should not be merged into one market.

questions.t: Benchmarking as a management method is credited to Robert C. Camp, who developed his ten-step process at Xerox.
questions.f: Benchmarking as a management method is credited to Robert C. Camp, who developed his ten-step process at General Electric.
questions.x: Camp's book laid out the ten steps he built at Xerox and tied them to Xerox's recovery after the late 1970s. L.L. Bean, IBM and Boeing were among the early adopters that followed.

questions.t: Functional benchmarking compares a function, such as logistics or billing, with firms in other industries that run similar processes.
questions.f: Functional benchmarking compares a function, such as logistics or billing, with similar units inside the same organization.
questions.x: Comparing similar units within one organization is internal benchmarking. Functional benchmarking looks outside the industry at firms that perform the same function well, which can surface bigger ideas but is harder to translate.

questions.t: Michael Porter argued that heavy benchmarking makes rivals more alike, a process he called competitive convergence.
questions.f: Michael Porter argued that heavy benchmarking makes rivals more distinct, a process he called competitive divergence.
questions.x: Porter saw benchmarking as improving operational effectiveness, but because best practices spread and are easy to copy, it pushes firms toward sameness. A sustainable advantage needs a distinct strategic position instead.

questions.t: If minimum average cost is reached only at a large share of market demand, an industry tends toward oligopoly.
questions.f: If minimum average cost is reached only at a small share of market demand, an industry tends toward oligopoly.
questions.x: Where the cost curve bottoms out relative to demand predicts how many efficient firms fit in the market. A small efficient size leaves room for many rivals; a large one supports only a few, and one bigger than demand points to a single producer.

questions.t: Diseconomies of scale arise mainly from coordination problems, as extra management layers and communication failures disrupt work.
questions.f: Diseconomies of scale arise mainly from spreading fixed costs over more units as output grows.
questions.x: Spreading fixed costs is a source of economies of scale, which lower unit cost. Diseconomies push average cost up as a firm grows, chiefly because coordinating a larger organization gets harder.

questions.t: Christensen and Greene's 1976 study found no significant scale economies for U.S. electricity generators above about 19 billion kWh a year.
questions.f: Christensen and Greene's 1976 study found scale economies kept growing for U.S. electricity generators well beyond 19 billion kWh a year.
questions.x: Their work is a classic sign that scale economies run out sooner than intuition suggests. Later studies questioned their data and assumptions, and a 2019 replication found returns to scale in U.S. generation declined from 1955 to 1996.

questions.t: Franco Modigliani and Merton Miller published their capital structure irrelevance result in the American Economic Review in 1958.
questions.f: Franco Modigliani and Merton Miller published their capital structure irrelevance result in the American Economic Review in 1972.
questions.x: Their June 1958 paper on the cost of capital launched modern corporate finance; follow-up essays came in 1963 and 1966. Modigliani won the Nobel prize in 1985 and Miller shared it in 1990.

questions.t: Under MM Proposition II, a levered firm's expected return on equity rises linearly with its debt-to-equity ratio.
questions.f: Under MM Proposition II, a levered firm's expected return on equity falls linearly as its debt-to-equity ratio rises.
questions.x: Adding debt makes the remaining equity riskier, so shareholders demand more. The higher cost of equity exactly offsets the cheaper debt, which is why the overall cost of capital stays the same.

questions.t: MM implies that a debt-funded recapitalization adds value only through a friction such as a tax shield or lower agency costs, not through leverage itself.
questions.f: MM implies that a debt-funded recapitalization adds value through leverage itself, because debt is cheaper than equity.
questions.x: In MM's frictionless world, investors can create leverage themselves, so they won't pay a premium for a firm doing it. Practitioners use the theorem to demand that any value claim name the imperfection responsible, such as taxes, distress costs or agency effects.

questions.t: Under the FAR, only warranted contracting officers may sign contracts for the government, and only within their written limits.
questions.f: Under the FAR, any agency program manager may sign contracts for the government, as long as funds are available.
questions.x: Contracting authority is personal and delegated through a written warrant, and a contracting officer can bind the government only within those limits. Program managers shape requirements but cannot obligate the government.

questions.t: FAR Parts 52 and 53 hold the standard solicitation provisions, contract clauses and forms that get written into actual contracts.
questions.f: FAR Parts 1 and 2 hold the standard solicitation provisions, contract clauses and forms that get written into actual contracts.
questions.x: The FAR has 53 parts: Parts 1-51 set policy across the acquisition life cycle, while Parts 52 and 53 supply the clauses and forms. Parts 1 and 2 cover the FAR system itself and definitions.

questions.t: GAO reported that the U.S. government committed about $793 billion on contracts in FY 2025.
questions.f: GAO reported that the U.S. government committed about $293 billion on contracts in FY 2025.
questions.x: GAO's May 2026 report put FY 2025 contract commitments near $793 billion, roughly $17.8 billion above FY 2024 after inflation. The figure shows why FAR rules shape the strategy of so many firms.

questions.t: In new-market disruption, an entrant first serves people who previously did without the product, as early personal computers did.
questions.f: In new-market disruption, an entrant first takes the least profitable customers of an existing market, as early personal computers did.
questions.x: Taking an incumbent's least profitable customers is low-end disruption, the path of steel minimills and discount retailers. New-market disruption competes against non-consumption, as PCs and Sony's pocket radios did.

questions.t: Christensen built disruptive innovation theory from evidence in the rigid disk-drive industry.
questions.f: Christensen built disruptive innovation theory from evidence in the semiconductor chip industry.
questions.x: In disk drives, incumbents led on capacity improvements their customers wanted, but entrants won each shift to smaller, initially weaker drives. That pattern became The Innovator's Dilemma (1997).

questions.t: A 2015 study by King and Baatartogtokh found only 9% of 77 cited disruption cases met all four core conditions they tested.
questions.f: A 2015 study by King and Baatartogtokh found 90% of 77 cited disruption cases met all four core conditions they tested.
questions.x: Their experts judged most of Christensen and Raynor's example cases a poor fit, though the authors suggested blending the theory with classic strategy rather than discarding it. Defenders replied that the theory has more than four elements.

questions.t: The balanced scorecard's four perspectives are financial, customer, internal business process, and learning and growth.
questions.f: The balanced scorecard's four perspectives are financial, customer, competitor, and learning and growth.
questions.x: Kaplan and Norton paired financial outcome measures with three perspectives that drive future results: customers, internal processes, and learning and growth. Competitors are not one of the four lenses.

questions.t: A key spur for the balanced scorecard was Analog Devices, whose quality measures all improved while its stock price fell by nearly 70%.
questions.f: A key spur for the balanced scorecard was Analog Devices, whose quality measures all worsened while its stock price rose by nearly 70%.
questions.x: Arthur Schneiderman showed the paradox at a 1990 project meeting: operational gains never linked to customer or financial outcomes didn't protect shareholder value. Kaplan and Norton published the scorecard in HBR in 1992.

questions.t: In a 2003 study of a bank's scorecard bonus plan, supervisors put more weight on financial measures, and the bank eventually dropped the scorecard.
questions.f: In a 2003 study of a bank's scorecard bonus plan, supervisors put more weight on nonfinancial measures, and the bank expanded the scorecard firm-wide.
questions.x: Ittner, Larcker and Meyer found supervisors favoured financial measures and used subjectivity to add or ignore others, prompting complaints of favouritism. It shows the risk of tying pay to an unweighted set of measures.

questions.t: Market segmentation is usually traced to Wendell Smith's 1956 Journal of Marketing article on differentiation and segmentation.
questions.f: Market segmentation is usually traced to Al Ries and Jack Trout's 1956 Journal of Marketing article on differentiation and segmentation.
questions.x: Wendell R. Smith argued in 1956 that products find their best markets by recognising differences between segments. Ries and Trout contributed positioning, first published in 1969 and popularised in the 1970s and 1980s.

questions.t: Good segmentation bases explain differences in how customers buy or use a product; demographics mostly serve as descriptors to find and reach segments.
questions.f: Good segmentation bases are demographics such as age and sex; buying and usage behavior mostly serve as descriptors to find and reach segments.
questions.x: Wind and Bell separate bases, which should predict response to marketing (usage, benefits sought, price sensitivity), from descriptors used to locate those customers. Age or sex alone often predicts response poorly.

questions.t: Yankelovich and Meer argued in 2006 that firms should keep segmentations for building brand identity separate from those for choosing markets and products.
questions.f: Yankelovich and Meer argued in 2006 that firms should use one psychographic segmentation for both building brand identity and choosing markets and products.
questions.x: They found demographic and psychographic segments, often reduced to ad personas, predicted purchases poorly. Their fix was to use different segmentations for different decisions rather than one for everything.

questions.t: Taiichi Ohno modelled Toyota's kanban system on American supermarkets, where shelves were refilled as customers took only what they needed.
questions.f: Taiichi Ohno modelled Toyota's kanban system on Ford's assembly lines, where shelves were refilled as workers took only what they needed.
questions.x: Ohno went to the U.S. to study Ford's mass production but took his key idea from supermarkets, where restocking matched what was taken. That pull logic is the heart of kanban.

questions.t: In a two-card kanban system, a withdrawal kanban lets the downstream stage take parts, and a production kanban authorizes upstream to replace them.
questions.f: In a two-card kanban system, a production kanban lets the downstream stage take parts, and a withdrawal kanban authorizes upstream to replace them.
questions.x: Withdrawal (transport) cards control how much moves downstream; production cards tell the upstream process to make exactly what was removed. Together they pull material through the line and cap work in process.

questions.t: Kanban is a pull system driven by actual consumption, in contrast to the forecast-driven push logic of material requirements planning.
questions.f: Kanban is a push system driven by a forecast schedule, much like the forecast-driven logic of material requirements planning.
questions.x: Kanban orders replacement parts only as parts are used, so production follows real demand. MRP pushes work through the plant from a forecast-based plan; single-card kanban systems sit between the two.

questions.t: George Stigler defined an entry barrier narrowly as a cost that entrants must bear but incumbents did not.
questions.f: Joe Bain defined an entry barrier narrowly as a cost that entrants must bear but incumbents did not.
questions.x: Bain (1956) used the broad test: anything letting incumbents keep above-normal profits without attracting entry. Stigler (1968) narrowed it to cost asymmetries, so scale economies available to all firms wouldn't count.

questions.t: Sunk costs deter entry because an incumbent can ignore money already sunk when pricing, while an entrant must still commit it.
questions.f: Sunk costs deter entry because an entrant can ignore money already sunk when pricing, while an incumbent must still commit it.
questions.x: The asymmetry means an entrant usually needs to be considerably more efficient than the incumbent to enter profitably. In contestability theory, scale economies deter entry only when combined with sunk costs.

questions.t: Under the 2023 DOJ and FTC Merger Guidelines, merging firms citing new entry must show it would be timely, likely and sufficient.
questions.f: Under the 2023 DOJ and FTC Merger Guidelines, merging firms citing new entry need only show that some entry is possible.
questions.x: Regulators ask not whether a barrier exists in the abstract but whether entry would actually restore competition. A history of absent or failed entry signals that entry will be slow or difficult.

questions.t: Psychological safety differs from group cohesiveness, which can suppress disagreement the way groupthink describes.
questions.f: Psychological safety is essentially group cohesiveness, which reliably encourages disagreement and dissent.
questions.x: Edmondson separated the two: a cohesive team may feel comfortable yet discourage dissent. Psychological safety is defined by the freedom to dissent, admit errors and challenge plans without punishment.

questions.t: Google's Project Aristotle ranked psychological safety first among five dynamics of effective teams, ahead of dependability.
questions.f: Google's Project Aristotle ranked dependability first among five dynamics of effective teams, ahead of psychological safety.
questions.x: Studying 180 teams, Google put psychological safety at the top, followed by dependability, structure and clarity, meaning, and impact. It adopted Edmondson's definition directly.

questions.t: A 2017 meta-analysis found psychological safety correlated far more with subjectively rated performance than with objective performance.
questions.f: A 2017 meta-analysis found psychological safety correlated far more with objective performance than with subjectively rated performance.
questions.x: Frazier and colleagues found a correlation of .40 with subjective ratings but only .07 with objective measures. Single-source, single-time designs also inflated effects, so causal claims stay weak.

questions.t: FASB Concepts Statements are nonauthoritative: they guide the Board when it writes standards but do not themselves establish GAAP.
questions.f: FASB Concepts Statements are authoritative: they sit in the Codification and establish GAAP that preparers must apply directly.
questions.x: The framework explains why standards look the way they do, but companies apply the standards, not the concepts. ASU 2024-02 even stripped remaining references to the Concepts Statements out of the Codification to keep that line clear.

questions.t: The FASB completed its rebuilt conceptual framework in July 2024 by issuing Chapter 6 of Concepts Statement No. 8, on measurement.
questions.f: The FASB completed its rebuilt conceptual framework in July 2024 by issuing Chapter 6 of Concepts Statement No. 8, on presentation.
questions.x: Measurement was the last piece of the project the Board reopened in 2014. Presentation was Chapter 7, issued earlier in December 2021 alongside Chapter 4 on the elements of financial statements.

questions.t: The FASB framework treats investors, lenders and other creditors as primary users because they usually cannot demand information directly from the company.
questions.f: The FASB framework treats regulators and tax authorities as primary users because they usually cannot demand information directly from the company.
questions.x: Chapter 1 sets the objective of general purpose reporting as helping capital providers decide whether to supply resources. Regulators can compel information, so they do not depend on general purpose reports the way outside capital providers do.

questions.t: Bebchuk, Cohen and Ferrell found that six entrenchment provisions drive the negative link between weak shareholder rights and firm value; the other 18 showed no such link.
questions.f: Bebchuk, Cohen and Ferrell found that 18 routine provisions drive the negative link between weak shareholder rights and firm value; the six entrenchment ones showed no such link.
questions.x: They decomposed the 24-provision Governance Index and found that staggered boards, poison pills, golden parachutes and similar shields against removal do the damage. The practical lesson is that a long governance checklist can mislead when a few provisions matter most.

questions.t: The UK's 1992 Cadbury Report followed the 1991 collapses of BCCI and Maxwell, which strengthened the case for common standards of accountability.
questions.f: The UK's 1992 Cadbury Report followed the 2001 collapses of Enron and WorldCom, which strengthened the case for common standards of accountability.
questions.x: Cadbury is seen as the starting point of modern UK governance codes, and it was a reaction to British scandals of 1991. Enron and WorldCom came a decade later and shaped US reform instead.

questions.t: Shleifer and Vishny's 1997 governance survey organized the field around two forces: legal protection of investors and concentration of ownership.
questions.f: Shleifer and Vishny's 1997 governance survey organized the field around two forces: board independence and the structure of executive pay.
questions.x: Their comparative lens explained why governance looks so different across countries: where law protects outside investors poorly, concentrated owners step in to monitor managers. Board make-up and pay are internal mechanisms, not the two forces they emphasized.

questions.t: Under the Sherman Act, naked price fixing among competitors is illegal per se, while most other restraints are judged under the rule of reason.
questions.f: Under the Sherman Act, naked price fixing among competitors is judged under the rule of reason, while most other restraints are illegal per se.
questions.x: Since Standard Oil (1911), courts ban only unreasonable restraints. Price fixing, market division and bid rigging are treated as so harmful that no justification is heard, while other conduct is weighed for its procompetitive and anticompetitive effects.

questions.t: The 1976 Hart-Scott-Rodino amendment to the Clayton Act requires parties to large mergers to notify the US government before closing.
questions.f: The 1936 Robinson-Patman amendment to the Clayton Act requires parties to large mergers to notify the US government before closing.
questions.x: Hart-Scott-Rodino created premerger notification so agencies can review big deals before they are done. Robinson-Patman is the earlier amendment, and it deals with price discrimination between merchants, not merger filings.

questions.t: Lina Khan's 2017 Yale Law Journal note argued that antitrust's focus on short-term prices cannot see the structural power of platforms such as Amazon.
questions.f: Carl Shapiro's 2017 Yale Law Journal note argued that antitrust's focus on short-term prices cannot see the structural power of platforms such as Amazon.
questions.x: Khan argued a platform can rationally price below cost to win lock-in and data, so a price test misses the harm. Shapiro was the cautious counterpoint: he backed tougher merger review but warned against stretching antitrust to target political power or inequality.

questions.t: In 1993 Gerstner reversed IBM's move toward autonomous, spin-off-ready business units and kept the company whole as an integrated IT provider.
questions.f: In 1993 Gerstner accelerated IBM's move toward autonomous, spin-off-ready business units and broke the company into independent firms.
questions.x: He reasoned that customers needed someone to assemble systems from many vendors, and IBM's breadth suited that role. He later called keeping IBM together his most important decision.

questions.t: By 2001, services and software together made up 58% of IBM's revenue, reflecting its shift from selling boxes to selling solutions.
questions.f: By 2001, services and software together made up 18% of IBM's revenue, reflecting its shift from selling boxes to selling solutions.
questions.x: Services brought in about $35 billion and software about $13 billion in 2001. That mix shows how far IBM had moved from a mainframe-dependent model where over 90% of profit once came from mainframes.

questions.t: Critics argue IBM's turnaround looks less impressive than Gerstner's memoir suggests, since a pension-plan change and large buybacks flattered results.
questions.f: Critics argue IBM's turnaround looks more impressive than Gerstner's memoir suggests, since a pension-plan change and large buybacks depressed results.
questions.x: The case leans heavily on insider accounts such as Who Says Elephants Can't Dance?. Skeptics add that shareholder-return figures look large partly because 1993 was such a low starting point.

questions.t: The word freemium was coined in 2006 by venture capitalist Fred Wilson together with Jarid Lukin, whom Wilson credited with proposing it.
questions.f: The word freemium was coined in 1996 by venture capitalist Fred Wilson together with Jarid Lukin, whom Wilson credited with proposing it.
questions.x: The term blends free and premium and dates from the mid-2000s web era of low-cost software distribution. Wilson popularized it but gave Lukin the credit for first suggesting the name.

questions.t: In freemium, a very high free-to-premium conversion rate can signal that the free offer is not attracting enough users.
questions.f: In freemium, a very high free-to-premium conversion rate can signal that the free tier gives away too much.
questions.x: The conversion rate works as a diagnostic in both directions. A low rate suggests the premium tier adds too little or the free tier is too generous, while a very high rate suggests the free funnel is too narrow to build a large base.

questions.t: In a National Academies Press experiment, adding a premium e-book raised paperback revenue more than adding a premium hardback did.
questions.f: In a National Academies Press experiment, adding a premium hardback raised paperback revenue more than adding a premium e-book did.
questions.x: Gu, Kannan and Ma found gains of 21.5% with the e-book versus 8.9% with the hardback, which they put down to compromise and attraction effects. They also warned that a cheaper premium option can cannibalize the existing paid product.

questions.t: A breakdown that is not mutually exclusive double-counts, while one that is not collectively exhaustive leaves gaps.
questions.f: A breakdown that is not mutually exclusive leaves gaps, while one that is not collectively exhaustive double-counts.
questions.x: Mutually exclusive means no item overlaps another, so overlap is what causes double-counting. Collectively exhaustive means the items cover the whole, so missing coverage is what leaves gaps.

questions.t: Barbara Minto coined the MECE acronym but attributes the underlying idea to Aristotle, claiming only its label and application to business writing.
questions.f: Barbara Minto coined the MECE acronym and claims the underlying idea as her own, rather than tracing it to an earlier thinker.
questions.x: Minto developed the rule while editing McKinsey reports and set it out in The Pyramid Principle (1985). She is explicit that the logic of exclusive, exhaustive groupings is ancient; her contribution was the shorthand and how she applied it.

questions.t: Charles Conn recommends making two or three different MECE cuts of the same problem, because a MECE breakdown is not unique and each cut surfaces different insights.
questions.f: Charles Conn recommends settling on a single MECE cut of a problem, because a correct MECE breakdown is unique and other cuts only repeat it.
questions.x: Many valid partitions exist for the same whole, and each highlights different levers. That is one limit of MECE: being exclusive and exhaustive guarantees clean addition, not the most useful framing.

questions.t: In buyouts, governance engineering means installing smaller, more active boards and replacing underperforming executives quickly.
questions.f: In buyouts, operational engineering means installing smaller, more active boards and replacing underperforming executives quickly.
questions.x: Sponsors are said to add value through financial, governance and operational engineering. Board and executive changes are governance engineering; operational engineering, more prominent since the 2000s, means bringing industry and operating expertise to the business.

questions.t: Kaplan's study of large 1980s management buyouts found capital spending fell and net cash flow rose in the three years after the deal.
questions.f: Kaplan's study of large 1980s management buyouts found capital spending rose and net cash flow fell in the three years after the deal.
questions.x: Across 76 buyouts from 1980 to 1986, operating income also rose and median market-adjusted value climbed 77%. Kaplan credited sharper incentives rather than layoffs or insiders exploiting shareholders.

questions.t: In the RJR Nabisco buyout, the roughly $10 billion premium paid to public shareholders shows that sellers can capture much of an LBO's gains when sponsors bid aggressively.
questions.f: In the RJR Nabisco buyout, the roughly $10 billion premium paid to public shareholders shows that sponsors keep most of an LBO's gains even when they bid aggressively.
questions.x: Value created by the buyout has to be split between the sellers and the sponsor. In KKR's 1988 deal, the bidding war pushed much of that value to RJR's public shareholders through the premium.

questions.t: On the FAR's best value continuum, the tradeoff process lets an agency pay more for a better proposal, while LPTA forbids tradeoffs altogether.
questions.f: On the FAR's best value continuum, LPTA lets an agency pay more for a better proposal, while the tradeoff process forbids paying above the lowest price.
questions.x: Tradeoff sits at the judgment-heavy end: an agency can award to a pricier offeror if the benefits merit the extra cost. LPTA sits at the price-driven end: among proposals that meet the technical bar, the lowest price wins.

questions.t: A tradeoff award decision must document the business judgments behind it, including benefits tied to extra cost, but the tradeoffs need not be quantified.
questions.f: A tradeoff award decision must quantify the dollar value of every tradeoff, but the business judgments behind it need not be documented.
questions.x: Because the method rests on subjective judgment, the written rationale is what protects the award. Protests of tradeoff awards usually turn on whether the record explains why a rival's advantages were or were not worth the price.

questions.t: In DRS Technical Services (2015), GAO denied the protest because the agency's record explained why DRS's technical strengths did not justify a premium of nearly $20 million.
questions.f: In DRS Technical Services (2015), GAO sustained the protest because the agency's record failed to explain why DRS's technical strengths did not justify a premium of nearly $20 million.
questions.x: DISA chose General Dynamics at about $132 million over the higher-rated DRS at about $152 million. GAO stressed that a selection official has broad discretion as long as the record explains the judgment.

questions.t: James March's 1991 paper argued that adaptive processes tend to refine exploitation faster than exploration, which pays off short term but becomes self-destructive long term.
questions.f: James March's 1991 paper argued that adaptive processes tend to refine exploration faster than exploitation, which pays off short term but becomes self-destructive long term.
questions.x: Exploitation pays back sooner and more surely, so organizations drift toward it. March's point is that this bias starves the search for new possibilities, the trade-off that ambidexterity later tried to solve.

questions.t: In contextual ambidexterity, leaders build a context of discipline, stretch, support and trust, and individuals decide how to split time between alignment and adaptation.
questions.f: In contextual ambidexterity, leaders assign exploration and exploitation to separate units, each with its own metrics, and integrate them at the senior-team level.
questions.x: Gibson and Birkinshaw proposed the contextual route as a complement to structural separation, which can isolate new-business groups from the core. Separate units linked at the top describe O'Reilly and Tushman's structural ambidexterity instead.

questions.t: Fujifilm began repositioning around 2000, when global film sales peaked, using film-related capabilities to enter cosmetics and pharmaceuticals, while Kodak stayed focused on film.
questions.f: Kodak began repositioning around 2000, when global film sales peaked, using film-related capabilities to enter cosmetics and pharmaceuticals, while Fujifilm stayed focused on film.
questions.x: The two firms had comparable technologies, yet Fujifilm grew into new businesses and Kodak went bankrupt in 2012. The contrast supports the view that incumbents fail through leadership and design, not missing technology.

questions.t: Andy Grove adapted OKRs at Intel from Peter Drucker's management by objectives, shifting the cycle from an annual rhythm to a quarterly one.
questions.f: Andy Grove adapted OKRs at Intel from Peter Drucker's management by objectives, shifting the cycle from a quarterly rhythm to an annual one.
questions.x: Drucker's 1950s MBO ran annually and was often tied to pay. Grove's version linked each objective to verifiable key results and ran faster, quarterly, so goals could track a fast-moving chip business.

questions.t: In Google's OKR playbook, committed OKRs are expected to score 1.0, while aspirational OKRs are expected to average about 0.7.
questions.f: In Google's OKR playbook, aspirational OKRs are expected to score 1.0, while committed OKRs are expected to average about 0.7.
questions.x: Committed OKRs are promises, so a miss calls for an explanation and a blameless postmortem. Aspirational OKRs describe a future without a clear path yet, so partial scores are normal and they roll forward until done.

questions.t: Ordóñez, Schweitzer, Galinsky and Bazerman argued in 2009 that specific, challenging goals can narrow focus and increase unethical behaviour, so they need careful dosing.
questions.f: Ordóñez, Schweitzer, Galinsky and Bazerman argued in 2009 that specific, challenging goals broaden focus and reduce unethical behaviour, so they need little oversight.
questions.x: They likened goals to prescription-strength medication whose side effects were overlooked, citing cases like the Ford Pinto. OKRs blunt part of this by decoupling goals from pay, but the narrow-focus risk remains.

questions.t: With constant margins and an infinite horizon, CLV equals margin times r/(1 + i − r), a multiple of about 4 at 90% retention and a 12% discount rate.
questions.f: With constant margins and an infinite horizon, CLV equals margin times r/(1 + i − r), a multiple of about 9 at 90% retention and a 12% discount rate.
questions.x: Plugging in gives 0.9 / (1.12 − 0.9) = 0.9 / 0.22, or roughly 4.1. The 9 confuses the retention rate with the multiple; discounting and the chance of defection both shrink the value of future margins.

questions.t: Reinartz and Kumar found long-standing customers were often not the most profitable, since they frequently paid less and were not cheaper to serve.
questions.f: Reinartz and Kumar found long-standing customers were usually the most profitable, since they frequently paid more and were cheaper to serve.
questions.x: Across four firms and over 16,000 customers, tenure and profit correlated only weakly. That challenges the retention-equals-profit story and is why they sort customers by both loyalty and profitability.

questions.t: In a newspaper study, subscribers acquired with a steep discount renewed at half the rate of regular-price subscribers and were worth about half as much.
questions.f: In a newspaper study, subscribers acquired with a steep discount renewed at twice the rate of regular-price subscribers and were worth about twice as much.
questions.x: Deep discounts attract customers who value the product less, so they lapse sooner. CLV makes this visible, which is why it is used to discipline promotions rather than judging them by sign-up volume alone.

questions.t: The engineering BOM reflects how parts relate to a product's functional design, while the manufacturing BOM reflects how they are actually assembled.
questions.f: The manufacturing BOM reflects how parts relate to a product's functional design, while the engineering BOM reflects how they are actually assembled.
questions.x: The MBOM is derived from the EBOM and defines what to make, while a separate bill of process defines how. Keeping the two in step when designs change is a recurring product-data task.

questions.t: A summarized BOM collapses the product tree so each item appears once with its total quantity, which suits purchasing and costing.
questions.f: An indented BOM collapses the product tree so each item appears once with its total quantity, which suits purchasing and costing.
questions.x: An indented, multilevel BOM keeps the family-tree shape, listing a shared part under every assembly that uses it. Collapsing that tree into totals per item is what makes the summarized view handy for buying and costing a plan.

questions.t: A 2009 MIT thesis found that inconsistent BOM structures across more than 50 Cisco business units led to product launch delays and higher support costs.
questions.f: A 2009 MIT thesis found that a single standard BOM structure across more than 50 Cisco business units led to product launch delays and higher support costs.
questions.x: Each unit had developed product-level BOMs its own way, and the inconsistency carried real costs. The author proposed a standardized, criteria-based workflow, showing that BOM structure is an organizational problem as much as a technical one.

questions.t: In Edmondson's 1996 hospital study, better-led nursing units recorded more medication errors, because their staff were more willing to report mistakes.
questions.f: In Edmondson's 1996 hospital study, better-led nursing units recorded fewer medication errors, because their staff made fewer mistakes.
questions.x: A detected error rate mixes how many errors happen with how willing people are to report them. This anomaly led to her work on psychological safety, and it warns managers not to read low reported numbers as good performance.

questions.t: In Edmondson's 1999 study of 51 work teams, team learning behavior mediated the link between psychological safety and team performance.
questions.f: In Edmondson's 1999 study of 51 work teams, team efficacy mediated the link between psychological safety and team performance.
questions.x: Safety made teams more willing to ask, admit errors and experiment, and that learning behavior is what improved performance. Team efficacy, by contrast, had no association with learning once safety was controlled for.

questions.t: In Edmondson's failure framework, intelligent failures are well-intentioned experiments in new territory, while basic failures are preventable slips.
questions.f: In Edmondson's failure framework, complex failures are well-intentioned experiments in new territory, while basic failures are preventable slips.
questions.x: Right Kind of Wrong (2023) separates basic, complex and intelligent failures. Complex failures have multiple causes and are reduced by catching small problems early; only intelligent failures generate useful knowledge worth encouraging.

questions.t: Teece's 2007 restatement split dynamic capabilities into sensing, seizing, and managing threats and reconfiguration.
questions.f: Teece's 2007 restatement split dynamic capabilities into sensing, scaling, and managing costs and consolidation.
questions.x: Sensing spots opportunities and threats, seizing commits investment to new products and business models, and reconfiguration keeps recombining assets so the base stays relevant. The skills and processes underneath are what he calls microfoundations.

questions.t: Eisenhardt and Martin (2000) argued dynamic capabilities share common features across firms, making them more substitutable and closer to best practice than Teece implied.
questions.f: Eisenhardt and Martin (2000) argued dynamic capabilities are unique to each firm, making them less substitutable and further from best practice than Teece implied.
questions.x: They treated dynamic capabilities as identifiable processes like product development and alliancing. Teece holds that widely known best practices are not dynamic capabilities because rivals can copy them, so this firm-specific versus best-practice dispute remains a core tension.

questions.t: Apple's iPod is used to illustrate dynamic capabilities: Apple sensed demand because existing MP3 players were bulky and unattractive, then seized it with a better-designed device.
questions.f: Apple's iPod is used to illustrate dynamic capabilities: Apple sensed demand because existing MP3 players were too expensive, then seized it with a cheaper device.
questions.x: The case maps onto all three clusters: sensing latent demand, seizing it with a smaller, better-designed product and a move into consumer electronics, and transforming the line through the Nano, Touch and iTunes.

questions.t: Freeman defined a stakeholder as any group or individual that can affect, or is affected by, the achievement of an organization's objectives.
questions.f: Freeman defined a stakeholder as any group or individual that holds a legal or financial claim on an organization's assets.
questions.x: The definition is deliberately broad, covering customers, employees, suppliers and communities as well as financiers. Its aim was to widen strategic management beyond a purely economic, owner-centred view.

questions.t: Donaldson and Preston's instrumental claim is that firms managing stakeholder relationships well perform better; their normative claim is that stakeholder interests have intrinsic value.
questions.f: Donaldson and Preston's normative claim is that firms managing stakeholder relationships well perform better; their instrumental claim is that stakeholder interests have intrinsic value.
questions.x: Their 1995 article split the theory into descriptive, instrumental and normative claims that must not be conflated. They saw the normative base as the most fundamental, which is why evidence that stakeholder management pays cannot settle whether it is right.

questions.t: The Business Roundtable's August 2019 purpose statement, signed by 181 CEOs, replaced statements issued since 1997 that had endorsed shareholder primacy.
questions.f: The Business Roundtable's August 2019 purpose statement, signed by 181 CEOs, reaffirmed statements issued since 1997 that had endorsed shareholder primacy.
questions.x: The statement committed signers to customers, employees, suppliers, communities and shareholders. Supporters called it a long-term commitment, while the Council of Institutional Investors warned it would give CEOs cover to evade shareholder oversight.

questions.t: The SEC recognized FASB pronouncements as authoritative US GAAP in Accounting Series Release No. 150 in December 1973.
questions.f: The SEC recognized FASB pronouncements as authoritative US GAAP in Accounting Series Release No. 150 in December 1959.
questions.x: The SEC had let the profession set standards since 1938, first through the Committee on Accounting Procedure and from 1959 the Accounting Principles Board. The FASB replaced the APB after the Wheat Commission urged a full-time independent body.

questions.t: A 2003 SEC staff study argued that bright-line GAAP thresholds let preparers engineer transactions to land on the preferred side of a line.
questions.f: A 2003 SEC staff study argued that bright-line GAAP thresholds stop preparers from engineering transactions to land on the preferred side of a line.
questions.x: Lease tests at 75% and 90% were a classic example: deals could be structured just under a threshold. The study recommended objectives-oriented standards grounded in a conceptual framework, not a swing to pure principles.

questions.t: Regulation G requires any public non-GAAP measure to be accompanied by the most directly comparable GAAP figure and a quantitative reconciliation.
questions.f: Regulation G requires any public non-GAAP measure to replace the most directly comparable GAAP figure, with no reconciliation needed.
questions.x: Adjusted metrics such as EBITDA are allowed, but readers must be able to see how they differ from GAAP. For analysts, that reconciliation is usually where judgment about true performance begins.

questions.t: Edward Mason introduced the structure-conduct-performance paradigm through case studies of single industries, and Joe Bain first applied it empirically across many industries.
questions.f: Joe Bain introduced the structure-conduct-performance paradigm through case studies of single industries, and Edward Mason first applied it empirically across many industries.
questions.x: Mason developed SCP at Harvard in 1939 and 1949 by studying industries one at a time. Bain's 1951 and 1956 work compared outcomes across many industries, turning the framework into cross-industry evidence.

questions.t: The SCP paradigm was criticized as descriptive rather than analytic, because its links between structure, conduct and performance were seldom derived from explicit models.
questions.f: The SCP paradigm was criticized as too abstract, because its links between structure, conduct and performance came from game-theoretic models rather than industry data.
questions.x: Without a model of how firms behave, cross-industry correlations could not show cause and effect. Critics like Stigler pushed for models built on maximizing behavior, and the field later rebuilt itself on game theory and structural econometrics.

questions.t: Tirole showed that capping a dominant firm's price can push it to cut costs yet also leave it excessive profits, so blanket rules help in some settings and backfire in others.
questions.f: Tirole showed that capping a dominant firm's price reliably removes its excess profits without changing its costs, so blanket rules work across all settings.
questions.x: His work, recognized with the 2014 economics prize, argued that good regulation must fit the industry. A cap lets the firm keep any savings it makes, which sharpens cost incentives but can leave large profits in place.

questions.t: Under an IDIQ contract, the government must order a stated minimum that is more than nominal but no more than it is fairly certain to need.
questions.f: Under an IDIQ contract, the government must order the stated maximum, which is set at the most it could conceivably need.
questions.x: The minimum is the only quantity the government owes; anything beyond it is ordered through task or delivery orders as needs arise. The maximum is a reasonable ceiling based on market research, not a commitment.

questions.t: The Federal Acquisition Streamlining Act of 1994 created a preference for multiple-award IDIQs and gave each holder a fair opportunity to be considered for orders.
questions.f: The Federal Acquisition Streamlining Act of 1994 created a preference for single-award IDIQs and gave the incumbent holder first claim on all orders.
questions.x: FASA pushed agencies to award several contracts so orders would still be competed among holders. Its exceptions, such as unusual urgency or logical follow-on orders, remain the core of today's fair-opportunity rules.

questions.t: GAO found that about 60% of IDIQ dollars in FY2011–FY2015 went through single-award contracts, despite the FAR's preference for multiple awards.
questions.f: GAO found that about 60% of IDIQ dollars in FY2011–FY2015 went through multiple-award contracts, in line with the FAR's preference for multiple awards.
questions.x: This gap is the main critique of IDIQs: weak competition. Single awards raise the risk of vendor lock-in, and GAO also found that 10 of 18 sampled DoD single-award contracts were not competed.

questions.t: Burgelman found that Intel's resource-allocation rules shifted fab capacity toward microprocessors before top management formally changed strategy.
questions.f: Burgelman found that Intel's top management formally changed strategy toward microprocessors before its resource-allocation rules shifted any fab capacity.
questions.x: Allocating scarce capacity by profitability moved the firm out of DRAMs from the middle up, while the stated strategy lagged. That made Intel a standard example of strategy emerging bottom-up through an internal selection environment.

questions.t: Intel regained manufacturing parity with Japanese chipmakers by the early 1990s by adopting Japanese production methods and standardizing its factories.
questions.f: Intel regained manufacturing parity with Japanese chipmakers by the early 1990s by outsourcing wafer fabrication to Japanese partners.
questions.x: Lécuyer shows that after 1985 management treated manufacturing weakness as a survival threat. Engineers adopted Japanese routines, put fabrication on a more scientific footing and improved transfer from development to production, a reform that took most of a decade.

questions.t: The Intel Inside program, launched in 1991, subsidized PC makers that put the Intel logo on their machines and in their advertising.
questions.f: The Intel Inside program, launched in 1991, charged PC makers a fee to put the Intel logo on their machines and in their advertising.
questions.x: Intel was known to manufacturers but invisible to consumers, so it paid co-op subsidies to get its brand in front of buyers. By the end of 1992 over 500 OEMs had joined, making it the textbook case of ingredient branding.

questions.t: During its patent years, Gillette sold its razor at a high price, launching a low-priced razor only after the patents expired in 1921.
questions.f: During its patent years, Gillette gave its razor away cheaply, launching a high-priced razor only after the patents expired in 1921.
questions.x: Randal Picker showed Gillette charged $5 for a razor with 12 blades from 1904, while rivals sold handles for about $1. The $1 Brownie razor came in 1921, so the founding legend of cheap razors and dear blades does not fit the record.

questions.t: The razor-and-blades model works as price discrimination: a low base price draws in light users, while consumable margins extract more from heavy users.
questions.f: The razor-and-blades model works as price discrimination: a low consumable price draws in heavy users, while base-product margins extract more from light users.
questions.x: Economists treat it as a two-part tariff, with the base product as an entry fee and the consumable as a per-use charge. Since heavy users buy more consumables, they pay more in total for the same base product.

questions.t: Schmalensee's 2015 analysis found pricing the razor below cost is never optimal in a standard continuum model and optimal only in a narrow two-type case.
questions.f: Schmalensee's 2015 analysis found pricing the razor below cost is always optimal in a standard continuum model and suboptimal only in a narrow two-type case.
questions.x: Building on Oi's 1971 result that the consumable should be priced above cost, he concluded below-cost razors are unlikely to be optimal in practice. He also argued such pricing, when used to discriminate, should not automatically be treated as predatory.

questions.t: In Liedtka's hypothesis cycle, generation is the creative what-if step, while testing is the analytical if-then step that names data that would support or undermine the idea.
questions.f: In Liedtka's hypothesis cycle, testing is the creative what-if step, while generation is the analytical if-then step that names data that would support or undermine the idea.
questions.x: Running the two steps repeatedly lets a team sharpen its hypotheses while still exploring new ones. The hypothesis tells the team which analyses matter, so effort goes where the answer is likely to be.

questions.t: In a randomized trial of 116 Italian startups, founders taught to test hypotheses performed better early on and were more likely to pivot to a different idea.
questions.f: In a randomized trial of 116 Italian startups, founders taught to test hypotheses performed better early on and were less likely to pivot to a different idea.
questions.x: Camuffo, Cordova and Gambardella found the scientific approach helped founders read market signals with less bias, so they abandoned weak ideas sooner. Treated firms did not, however, drop out less often than the control group.

questions.t: Confirmation bias threatens hypothesis-driven teams because people testing a favored hypothesis tend to pick tests that can only return yes, as in Wason's 2-4-6 task.
questions.f: Confirmation bias threatens hypothesis-driven teams because people testing a favored hypothesis tend to pick tests that can only return no, as in Wason's 2-4-6 task.
questions.x: Committing early to an answer invites seeking only supporting evidence and explaining away contrary data. The standard remedy is to generate alternative hypotheses and design tests capable of refuting them.

questions.t: Black-Scholes combines a stock and its options into a riskless portfolio that must earn the risk-free rate, so no estimate of a risk premium is needed.
questions.f: Black-Scholes combines a stock and its options into a riskless portfolio that must earn the market's expected return, so an estimate of the risk premium is needed.
questions.x: If the hedged portfolio earned more than the risk-free rate, arbitrage would erase the excess. Continuous rebalancing turns that argument into a differential equation whose solution is the formula, with no view on investors' risk attitudes required.

questions.t: Shleifer and Vishny argued arbitrage can fail in extremes because investors pull money from arbitrageurs showing losses just as a mispricing widens.
questions.f: Shleifer and Vishny argued arbitrage is strongest in extremes because investors pour money into arbitrageurs just as a mispricing widens.
questions.x: Arbitrage is done mostly by specialists managing other people's money, and outside investors judge them on recent returns. The resulting withdrawals can force selling at the worst moment and even amplify price shocks.

questions.t: Froot and Dabora found that each of the Royal Dutch and Shell twin shares moved with the market where it traded most, despite pooled cash flows.
questions.f: Froot and Dabora found that each of the Royal Dutch and Shell twin shares moved with its own company's earnings, despite pooled cash flows.
questions.x: Because the twins shared cash flows at a fixed ratio, their prices should have moved in lockstep. The persistent, location-driven gaps are a classic anomaly for efficient markets and a showcase for the limits of arbitrage.

questions.t: In Competing Against Luck (2016), Christensen argued that understanding the job customers hire a product to do, rather than their demographics, makes innovation more predictable.
questions.f: In Competing Against Luck (2016), Christensen argued that understanding customers' demographics, rather than the job they hire a product to do, makes innovation more predictable.
questions.x: Jobs to be done shifts the focus from who the customer is to the progress they are trying to make. Christensen illustrated it with firms like Intuit, Airbnb and Chobani, and it was his second big idea after disruption.

questions.t: Historian Tom Nicholas argues that Christensen's disruption research drew on Alfred Chandler's account of the large, vertically integrated enterprise.
questions.f: Historian Tom Nicholas argues that Christensen's disruption research drew on Joseph Schumpeter's account of creative destruction.
questions.x: Christensen built theory from business history, starting with a 1993 Business History Review study of integrated disk-drive makers. Nicholas places that method in Chandler's tradition; creative destruction is a related idea, not the source he identifies.

questions.t: Christensen founded Innosight in 2000 to advise companies on innovation and Rose Park Advisors in 2007 to invest along the lines of his theories.
questions.f: Christensen founded Rose Park Advisors in 2000 to advise companies on innovation and Innosight in 2007 to invest along the lines of his theories.
questions.x: He turned his research into practice through a consultancy, an investment firm and a think tank now called the Christensen Institute. Innosight is the consulting arm; Rose Park is the investor.

questions.t: In hoshin kanri, catchball passes draft goals down, across and back up the organization so each level negotiates what it can achieve and what resources it needs.
questions.f: In hoshin kanri, catchball passes final goals down the organization once, so each level accepts its targets without negotiating what it can achieve or needs.
questions.x: Catchball is the method's distinctive mechanism: goals can change as levels push back. It is often run with an X-matrix and one-page A3 plans, which is also why it can be slow, as at Land Rover where it took 12 months.

questions.t: Hoshin kanri separates breakthrough objectives that need cross-functional change from daily management of routine indicators like quality, cost and delivery.
questions.f: Hoshin kanri merges breakthrough objectives that need cross-functional change into daily management of routine indicators like quality, cost and delivery.
questions.x: The few breakthrough objectives get deployed and reviewed through the strategy cycle, while routine KPIs are run as daily management. Keeping them apart stops a handful of strategic priorities from drowning among many operational metrics.

questions.t: Witcher notes that hoshin kanri is nearly absent from mainstream strategy texts, partly because outsiders see it as mechanistic and tool-heavy.
questions.f: Witcher notes that hoshin kanri dominates mainstream strategy texts, partly because insiders see it as flexible and light on tools.
questions.x: Its literature sits mainly in quality and operations management. Its inside-out, process-driven logic also fits awkwardly with market-positioning views of strategy, which dominate strategy textbooks.

questions.t: Cannibalization slows incumbents' adoption of new technology, while preemption, the motive to launch before rivals can, speeds it up.
questions.f: Preemption slows incumbents' adoption of new technology, while cannibalization, the motive to launch before rivals can, speeds it up.
questions.x: An incumbent launching a new technology mostly replaces its own profit stream, so its net gain is smaller than a start-up's. Preemption pushes the other way, since waiting lets rivals take the new market.

questions.t: Igami's 2017 study of hard disk drive makers found cannibalization explained at least 57% of the gap between incumbent and entrant innovation.
questions.f: Igami's 2017 study of hard disk drive makers found cannibalization explained at most 17% of the gap between incumbent and entrant innovation.
questions.x: Even with strong preemptive motives and a cost advantage, incumbents held back because new products would eat their existing profits. Igami read this as rational incumbent behavior rather than the managerial blindness Christensen stressed.

questions.t: Newspapers whose websites closely copied the print edition were far more likely to lose circulation, suggesting differentiation, not abstention, limits channel cannibalization.
questions.f: Newspapers whose websites differed most from the print edition were far more likely to lose circulation, suggesting abstention, not differentiation, limits channel cannibalization.
questions.x: Deleersnyder and colleagues found most papers suffered no significant slowdown from adding a website. Those that did had much higher content overlap with print, about 78% versus 45%.

questions.t: The term enterprise resource planning was coined by research firm Gartner in the early 1990s for integrated software reaching beyond the factory.
questions.f: The term enterprise resource planning was coined by software maker SAP in the early 1970s for integrated software reaching beyond the factory.
questions.x: ERP grew out of MRP in the 1970s and MRP II after it, but the name came later, from an analyst firm describing cross-functional packages. SAP was founded in 1972, and its R/3 system arrived in 1992.

questions.t: Of the three ERP implementation activities, tailoring with custom code is the costliest and riskiest, so firms tend to favor process adaptation and configuration.
questions.f: Of the three ERP implementation activities, configuring parameters is the costliest and riskiest, so firms tend to favor tailoring with custom code.
questions.x: Lorenzo, Kawalek and Wood-Harper distinguish redesigning processes, configuring the package and tailoring it. Custom code is expensive to build and maintain, which is why adopters usually bend their processes to the standard software instead.

questions.t: Hitt, Wu and Zhou found that ERP adopters' productivity rose during implementation and dipped afterwards.
questions.f: Hitt, Wu and Zhou found that ERP adopters' productivity dipped during implementation and rose afterwards.
questions.x: Their 2002 study of SAP R/3 adopters also found higher productivity and a Tobin's q about 13% above non-adopters. The authors cautioned that long-run effects needed more post-implementation data and that the sample covered only one vendor.

questions.t: Google's Project Oxygen, which preceded Aristotle, set out to prove managers did not matter and found instead that better managers were linked to lower turnover.
questions.f: Google's Project Oxygen, which preceded Aristotle, set out to prove managers mattered and found instead that manager quality had no link to turnover.
questions.x: Oxygen began in 2009 as a skeptical test and ended by distilling eight behaviors of good managers that Google built into feedback and training. Aristotle then applied the same evidence-driven approach to teams.

questions.t: In Project Aristotle, team size, colocation and seniority did not significantly predict team effectiveness at Google.
questions.f: In Project Aristotle, team size, colocation and seniority were the strongest predictors of team effectiveness at Google.
questions.x: The study's headline was that how a team works together matters more than who is on it. Google cautioned that these composition factors might still matter in other organizations.

questions.t: Woolley and colleagues found in 2010 that a group's collective intelligence tracked members' social sensitivity and evenly shared turns, not their individual intelligence.
questions.f: Woolley and colleagues found in 2010 that a group's collective intelligence tracked members' maximum individual intelligence, not their social sensitivity or turn-taking.
questions.x: This independent lab result points the same way as Aristotle: process beats composition. A team of the smartest individuals does not automatically think best together.

questions.t: Lieberman and Montgomery's 1988 Strategic Management Journal article reviewed both the advantages and disadvantages of pioneering, critiquing the belief that being first pays.
questions.f: Golder and Tellis's 1988 Strategic Management Journal article reviewed both the advantages and disadvantages of pioneering, critiquing the belief that being first pays.
questions.x: The Stanford pair popularized the term while questioning an idea business schools had taken for granted. Golder and Tellis came later, in 1993, with a historical study of about 500 brands.

questions.t: Golder and Tellis argued earlier pioneer studies were inflated by survivor bias, since failed pioneers were missing from the data; in their sample 47% of pioneers failed.
questions.f: Golder and Tellis argued earlier pioneer studies were deflated by survivor bias, since failed followers were missing from the data; in their sample 47% of followers failed.
questions.x: Databases like PIMS only saw firms still around, so they overstated pioneers' lasting share leads. Golder and Tellis found pioneers averaged about 10% share, versus roughly 30% in earlier work.

questions.t: A first mover can preempt scarce assets such as shelf space, distribution channels and attractive product positions before rivals arrive.
questions.f: A fast follower can preempt scarce assets such as shelf space, distribution channels and attractive product positions before the pioneer arrives.
questions.x: Preemption is one producer-side source of pioneer advantage, alongside moving down the experience curve first. Followers instead gain by learning from the pioneer's mistakes and entering once demand and technology are clearer.

questions.t: The ESG label grew out of the UN Global Compact's Who Cares Wins report, endorsed in 2004 by 18 financial institutions from nine countries.
questions.f: The ESG label grew out of the UN Global Compact's Who Cares Wins report, endorsed in 1994 by 18 financial institutions from nine countries.
questions.x: The report's signatories, including Goldman Sachs, HSBC and UBS, managed over $6 trillion. Its aim was to bring environmental, social and governance issues into mainstream analysis rather than leave them to ethical-investing niches.

questions.t: Berg, Kölbel and Rigobon found that measurement differences, not weighting, explained most of the divergence among six major ESG ratings.
questions.f: Berg, Kölbel and Rigobon found that weighting differences, not measurement, explained most of the divergence among six major ESG ratings.
questions.x: Measurement accounted for 56% of the disagreement, scope for 38% and weighting for only 6%. Raters disagree mainly on how they assess the same attribute, which is why ESG labels can give investors noisy signals.

questions.t: Of the ISSB's June 2023 standards, IFRS S1 sets general sustainability disclosure requirements, while IFRS S2 adds climate-specific disclosures.
questions.f: Of the ISSB's June 2023 standards, IFRS S2 sets general sustainability disclosure requirements, while IFRS S1 adds climate-specific disclosures.
questions.x: S1 covers sustainability-related risks and opportunities over the short, medium and long term, and S2 fully incorporates the TCFD recommendations. Both are built around investor decision-usefulness, like financial-reporting standards.

questions.t: Indirect network effects work through complements: as more of a hardware product sells, more software or content is made for it, raising the hardware's value.
questions.f: Direct network effects work through complements: as more of a hardware product sells, more software or content is made for it, raising the hardware's value.
questions.x: Katz and Shapiro separated direct effects, from physical connection as with telephones or fax machines, from indirect ones that flow through complementary goods. They also named a third channel, denser post-purchase service for larger installed bases.

questions.t: In Katz and Shapiro's model, firms with large networks tend to resist compatibility even when it would raise welfare, while firms with small networks favor it.
questions.f: In Katz and Shapiro's model, firms with small networks tend to resist compatibility even when it would raise welfare, while firms with large networks favor it.
questions.x: Compatibility shares the benefit of a big installed base with rivals, so the leader loses an advantage and the laggard gains one. That is why standards fights pit large incumbents against smaller challengers.

questions.t: Liebowitz and Margolis disputed that QWERTY was demonstrably inferior to Dvorak or that Betamax was clearly better than VHS, challenging famous lock-in stories.
questions.f: Liebowitz and Margolis confirmed that QWERTY was demonstrably inferior to Dvorak and that Betamax was clearly better than VHS, supporting famous lock-in stories.
questions.x: They argued network externalities that cause real market failure are theoretically fragile and empirically undocumented. Many networks need only a critical mass, and participants can often internalize the benefits.

questions.t: Amazon's free cash flow fell to $11.2 billion in FY2025 from $38.2 billion in 2024, because capital spending surged even as operating cash flow rose.
questions.f: Amazon's free cash flow fell to $11.2 billion in FY2025 from $38.2 billion in 2024, because operating cash flow fell even as capital spending held steady.
questions.x: Operating cash flow grew from about $116 billion to $140 billion, but net property and equipment purchases jumped from about $78 billion to $128 billion. Reading the drop as operating weakness would misread a deliberate investment surge.

questions.t: Lehn and Poulsen linked undistributed cash flow to going-private deals in 1980–1987, with the effect strongest where managers owned little equity.
questions.f: Lehn and Poulsen linked undistributed cash flow to going-private deals in 1980–1987, with the effect strongest where managers owned large equity stakes.
questions.x: Surplus cash also predicted the premium paid to shareholders. The result fits Jensen's agency view: managers with little stake are most tempted to waste free cash, so buyouts that force it out create the most value there.

questions.t: Unlike free cash flow, EBITDA makes no deduction for capital expenditures or changes in working capital.
questions.f: Unlike EBITDA, free cash flow makes no deduction for capital expenditures or changes in working capital.
questions.x: Free cash flow starts from operating cash flow, which already reflects working-capital changes, and then subtracts capital spending. That makes it a closer gauge of cash a business can actually return or redeploy than EBITDA.

questions.t: Kodak engineer Steven Sasson built a digital camera prototype in 1975, which Kodak patented in 1978 but never produced.
questions.f: Fujifilm engineer Steven Sasson built a digital camera prototype in 1975, which Fujifilm patented in 1978 but never produced.
questions.x: The device stored 100 × 100 pixel black-and-white images on cassette tape and took about 23 seconds per shot. That Kodak invented the technology that undermined it is why the case is a strategy-teaching staple.

questions.t: Vinokurova and Kapoor argue Kodak saw digital coming and invested in it, but film's exceptional profitability set aspirations few new ventures could meet.
questions.f: Vinokurova and Kapoor argue Kodak ignored digital and never invested in it, because film's exceptional profitability made new ventures seem unnecessary.
questions.x: Kodak tried Photo CD, APS, digital cameras and inkjet. Uncertain timing of consumer adoption and an illusion of resilience from strong film sales made unprofitable digital bets hard to sustain, a richer story than simple myopia.

questions.t: Kodak's 2007 move into consumer inkjet printers bet that people would keep printing photos even from digital cameras.
questions.f: Kodak's 2007 move into consumer inkjet printers bet that people would stop printing photos and view them on screens instead.
questions.x: The bet extended Kodak's prints-and-consumables model into the digital era. Funding inkjet while closing film plants strained cash before the 2012 bankruptcy, and the assumption failed as photos moved to screens.

questions.t: In NIST's cloud models, PaaS customers deploy their own applications on the provider's platform, while IaaS customers rent raw computing, storage and networking.
questions.f: In NIST's cloud models, IaaS customers deploy their own applications on the provider's platform, while PaaS customers rent raw computing, storage and networking.
questions.x: The three models differ by how much the customer controls. In SaaS it controls almost nothing beyond user settings, in PaaS it brings its own applications, and in IaaS it runs whatever software it likes on rented infrastructure.

questions.t: Because SaaS subscription revenue is recognized ratably over the contract term, a slump in new bookings shows up in reported revenue only gradually.
questions.f: Because SaaS subscription revenue is recognized upfront at contract signing, a slump in new bookings shows up in reported revenue immediately.
questions.x: Each contract's revenue is spread across its 12 to 36 month term, so reported revenue lags bookings. Cash billed annually in advance meanwhile builds a large deferred revenue balance on the balance sheet.

questions.t: In fiscal 2026, subscription and support made up about 95% of Salesforce's $41.5 billion in total revenue.
questions.f: In fiscal 2026, subscription and support made up about 65% of Salesforce's $41.5 billion in total revenue.
questions.x: Subscription and support brought in about $39.4 billion of the total. That near-total reliance on recurring fees is what defines a mature SaaS model, in contrast with old licence-and-maintenance software revenue.

questions.t: Chevallier advises building the diagnostic why tree before the solution how tree, because understanding causes sharpens the question the solution tree answers.
questions.f: Chevallier advises building the solution how tree before the diagnostic why tree, because listing options sharpens the question the diagnostic tree answers.
questions.x: A why tree maps root causes of an outcome, and a how tree maps options for reaching a goal. Neither is superior, but solving before diagnosing risks answering the wrong question, and each tree should hold only one type of question.
